objects.definition:
typedef struct _Iso9660PVD
{
	uint8_t   VDType;                          // (00) Must be 1 for primary volume descriptor.
	char      VSStdId[5];                      // (01) Must be "CD001".
	uint8_t   VSStdVersion;                    // (06) Must be 1.
	uint8_t   volumeFlags;                     // (07) 0 in primary volume descriptor.
	char      systemIdentifier[32];            // (08) What system this CD-ROM is meant for.
	char      volumeIdentifier[32];            // (28) The volume name.
	char      Reserved2[8];                    // (48) Must be 0's.
	uint32_t  lsbVolumeSpaceSize;              // (50) Volume size, least-significant-byte order.
	uint32_t  msbVolumeSpaceSize;              // (54) Volume size, most-significant-byte order.
	char      escapeSequences[32];             // (58) 0's in primary volume descriptor
	uint16_t  lsbVolumeSetSize;                // (78) Number of volumes in volume set (must be 1).
	uint16_t  msbVolumeSetSize;                // (7A)
	uint16_t  lsbVolumeSetSequenceNumber;      // (7C) Which volume in volume set (not used).
	uint16_t  msbVolumeSetSequenceNumber;      // (7E)
	uint16_t  lsbLogicalBlockSize;             // (80) We'll assume 2048 for block size.
	uint16_t  msbLogicalBlockSize;             // (82)
	uint32_t  lsbPathTableSize;                // (84) How many bytes in path table.
	uint32_t  msbPathTableSize;                // (88)
	uint32_t  lsbPathTable1;                   // (8C) Mandatory occurrence.
	uint32_t  lsbPathTable2;                   // (90) Optional occurrence.
	uint32_t  msbPathTable1;                   // (94) Mandatory occurrence.
	uint32_t  msbPathTable2;                   // (98) Optional occurrence.
	uint8_t   rootDirectoryRecord[34];         // (9C) Duplicate root directory entry.
	char      volumeSetIdentifier[128];        // (BE) Various copyright and control fields follow. */
	char      publisherIdentifier[128];        // (13E)
	char      dataPreparerIdentifier[128];     // (1BE)
	char      applicationIdentifier[128];      // (23E)
	char      copyrightFileIdentifier[37];     // (2BE)
	char      abstractFileIdentifier[37];      // (2E3)
	char      bibliographicFileIdentifier[37]; // (308)
	char      volumeCreation[17];              // (32D)
	char      volumeModification[17];          // (33E)
	char      volumeExpiration[17];            // (34F)
	char      volumeEffective[17];             // (360)
	uint8_t   FileStructureStandardVersion;    // (371)
	char      Reserved4;                       // (372) Must be 0.
	char      ApplicationUse[512];             // (373)
	char      FutureStandardization[653];      // (573)
} __attribute__((packed)) Iso9660PVD;
objects.description: Packed Primary Volume Descriptor structure for ISO 9660 images. Represents the on-disk PVD sector with both LSB/MSB duplicated numeric fields and fixed-size text fields. Intended to be read directly from disk as-is.

objects.definition:
typedef struct _Iso9660DirectoryRecord
{
	uint8_t   len_dr;          // (00) Directory record length.
	uint8_t   XARlength;       // (01) Extended attribute record length.
	uint32_t  lsbStart;        // (02) First logical block where file starts.
	uint32_t  msbStart;        // (06)
	uint32_t  lsbDataLength;   // (0A) Number of bytes in file.
	uint32_t  msbDataLength;   // (0E)
	uint8_t   year;            // (12) Since 1900.
	uint8_t   month;           // (13)
	uint8_t   day;             // (14)
	uint8_t   hour;            // (15)
	uint8_t   minute;          // (16)
	uint8_t   second;          // (17)
	uint8_t   gmtOffset;       // (18) 15-minute offset from Universal Time.
	uint8_t   fileFlags;       // (19) Attributes of a file or directory.
	uint8_t   interleaveSize;  // (1A) Used for interleaved files.
	uint8_t   interleaveSkip;  // (1B) Used for interleaved files.
	uint16_t  lsbVolSetSeqNum; // (1C) Which volume in volume set contains this file.
	uint16_t  msbVolSetSeqNum; // (1E)
	uint8_t   len_fi;          // (20) Length of file identifier that follows.
	char      fi;              // (21) File identifier (variable length)
} __attribute__((packed)) Iso9660DirectoryRecord;
objects.description: Packed ISO 9660 directory record structure representing a single directory entry with dual-endian numeric fields and a variable-length file identifier. Designed to map directly to on-disk directory records.
Packed ISO 9660 path table record describing a directory entry in the path table, including identifier length, location, parent number, and a variable-length identifier field.
Enumeration of command opcodes for the NetISO network protocol used to manipulate files and directories remotely.
Generic 16-byte command frame carrying an opcode and 14 bytes of payload for miscellaneous requests.
Command to open/stat a file for reading; includes opcode and file path length (fp_len).
Result of open/stat operation with file size (-1 on error) and modification time.
Critical read command with byte count and file offset; server exits on read failure.
Critical read command for 2048-byte sectors from a 2352-sector ISO, with start sector and count.
Non-critical read command specifying number of bytes and offset; returns a separate result followed by data.
Result indicating number of bytes read for a non-critical read operation; -1 on error.
Command to create/truncate a file for writing; includes file path length.
Result of file create/truncate operation; 0 on success, -1 on error.
Command to write data to the active write-only file; num_bytes indicates payload size sent after the command.
Result indicating number of bytes written; -1 on error.
Command to open a directory; includes directory path length (dp_len).
Result of opening a directory; 0 on success, -1 on error.
Command to read the next entry from the active directory stream.
Result for a directory entry with size, filename length, and directory flag; -1 size indicates end/error.
Extended directory entry result including size and timestamps (mtime, ctime, atime), filename length, and directory flag.
Result indicating total number of bytes to follow for a complete directory listing; -1 on error (implied by protocol, though not stated).
One entry in the bulk directory listing, including size, mtime, directory flag, and null-terminated name up to 512 bytes.
Command to delete a file; includes file path length.
Result of delete operation; 0 success, -1 error (implied; exact semantics not fully documented).
Command to create a directory; includes directory path length.
Result of mkdir; 0 success, -1 error (implied).
Command to remove an empty directory; includes directory path length.
Result of rmdir; 0 success, -1 error (implied).
Command to stat a file or directory; includes path length.
Result of stat with size, timestamps (mtime, ctime, atime), and directory flag. Size -1 indicates error.
Command to compute the size of a directory; includes directory path length.
Result containing total directory size in bytes; -1 on error.

32-bit unsigned integer type referenced by the PADLOCK_ALIGN16 macro via a cast. It is not defined in this header; it is normally provided by <inttypes.h> or <stdint.h>. Included here only to note usage; no definition is present in this file.

Opaque-like context holding AES round count, pointer to round keys, and an internal buffer. It is used with aes_setkey_enc/dec to prepare for encryption/decryption and then passed to the various AES crypt functions. Callers are expected to allocate it (stack or heap) and initialize it via aes_setkey_enc or aes_setkey_dec before use. Destruction requires no special API; zeroizing is recommended if sensitive.

Pure-virtual interface for file-like I/O. It models open/close/read/write/seek and a stat-like query, and exposes a ps3Mode flag. Must be subclassed to provide concrete behavior; instances are managed via pointers or references to this interface. Construction and destruction are via derived classes; the virtual destructor allows safe deletion through this interface pointer. The referenced file_stat_t and some parameter types are declared elsewhere.

Struct describing a contiguous address region on a PS3 ISO and whether it is encrypted. Addresses are absolute byte addresses (not LBA). Used to decide when decryption should be applied for read ranges.
Enumeration of supported PS3 disc encryption types: none, 3k3y decrypted, 3k3y encrypted, and Redump encrypted. Guides decryption behavior in File.

Concrete file implementation extending AbstractFile with support for multi-part ISOs and optional PS3 ISO decryption (3k3y/Redump). Manages OS file handles, read/write/seek, and decryption state (encryption type, regions, AES context, IV).
Linked-list node describing a file entry to be placed in the ISO image. Holds path, lengths, starting LBA (rlba), size, a multipart flag, and link to next node.

Linked-list node describing a directory to be included in the ISO image. Stores path info, prebuilt directory record content for standard and Joliet, sizes, an index, a list of contained files, and link to next directory.
Represents a contiguous sector range by inclusive start and end sector numbers, likely for describing unencrypted areas.
Structure stored on disc describing up to 255 unencrypted sector ranges. The 'zero' field is always set to 0 per comment.
Fixed-size (0x200 bytes) structure representing a PS3 disc information sector, including console/product IDs, padding zeros, an info block, and a hash of the info block.

Concrete file-like class for building and writing ISO 9660 (and Joliet) images, tailored for PS3 mode support. Owns buffers, path tables, and directory/file lists; provides AbstractFile-compatible I/O plus generation methods (build, write, generate). Construction requires a bool ps3Mode; destruction frees managed resources (details not shown).

functions.name: create_start_thread
functions.description: Creates a new thread and immediately starts it running start_routine with the provided arg. The created thread handle/ID is returned via the thread output parameter. Intended as a cross-platform wrapper over pthread_create (POSIX) or CreateThread/begin-thread equivalents (Windows). Return value semantics are not documented here; typical behavior is 0 on success and nonzero on failure, but this is unknown without source.
requirements: thread must be a non-null pointer to storage for the resulting thread_t.
start_routine must be a non-null function pointer of type void* (*)(void*).
arg is passed verbatim to start_routine and may be NULL.
The caller must ensure any data referenced by arg remains valid for at least the time start_routine accesses it.
The returned thread must be joined or otherwise cleaned up using join_thread or the platform-appropriate mechanism to avoid resource leaks (inferred from typical usage).
Return/error codes are not specified in this header; callers must be prepared for unknown conventions (e.g., 0 vs. nonzero for success/failure).

functions.name: join_thread
functions.description: Waits for the specified thread to terminate and joins it, providing cross-platform behavior similar to pthread_join (POSIX) or WaitForSingleObject/CloseHandle (Windows). Return value semantics are not documented here; typical behavior would indicate success/failure, but this is unknown without source.
requirements: thread must identify a valid, joinable thread previously created by create_start_thread in the current process.
The calling thread must not attempt to join itself (general threading constraint; exact enforcement unknown).
The function blocks until the target thread finishes executing.
Return/error codes are not specified in this header; callers must be prepared for unknown conventions.

functions.name: open_file
functions.description: Opens the file at path with the specified flags and returns a platform-abstracted file handle (file_t). On POSIX, file_t is an int (file descriptor); on Windows, file_t is a HANDLE. Acts as a cross-platform wrapper around open/CreateFile-like APIs with oflag controlling access and creation mode. Exact flag mapping and error handling are not documented here.
requirements: path must be a non-null, null-terminated string.

oflag must contain valid open flags for the implementation; typical POSIX-style flags (e.g., O_RDONLY, O_WRONLY, O_RDWR, O_CREAT) are implied by including <fcntl.h>, but the exact accepted values on Windows are unknown.
On success, the returned file_t should satisfy FD_OK(fd) according to the header; INVALID_FD indicates failure.
Callers must later close the returned handle using close_file to avoid resource leaks.

functions.name: close_file
functions.description: Closes a previously opened file handle obtained from open_file, releasing underlying OS resources. Cross-platform wrapper around close (POSIX) or CloseHandle (Windows). Return value semantics are not documented here.
requirements: fd must be a valid file handle returned by open_file and must satisfy FD_OK(fd).
The caller must not use fd after a successful close_file call.
Return/error codes are not specified in this header; callers must be prepared for unknown conventions.

functions.name: read_file
functions.signature: ssize_t read_file(file_t fd, void *buf, size_t nbyte);
functions.description: Reads up to nbyte bytes from the file referred to by fd into the buffer buf. Cross-platform wrapper resembling POSIX read. Returns a byte count (ssize_t), where negative values typically indicate an error; exact semantics and partial read behavior are not documented here.
requirements: fd must be a valid, open file handle supporting read operations.
buf must be a non-null pointer to a writable memory region of at least nbyte bytes.
nbyte may be zero; behavior should be consistent with underlying OS read semantics (unknown specifics).
The current file offset is advanced by the number of bytes read (inferred from typical read semantics).
On end-of-file, typical behavior is to return 0; exact behavior is not specified here.
Error reporting conventions (e.g., negative return, errno) are not specified; callers must handle unknown conventions.

functions.name: write_file
functions.signature: ssize_t write_file(file_t fd, void *buf, size_t nbyte);
functions.description: Writes up to nbyte bytes from the buffer buf to the file referred to by fd. Cross-platform wrapper resembling POSIX write. Returns a byte count (ssize_t), where negative values typically indicate an error; exact semantics and partial write behavior are not documented here. Note: buf is not const in this declaration, which is unusual; whether the buffer may be modified by the implementation is unknown.
requirements: fd must be a valid, open file handle supporting write operations.

buf must be a non-null pointer to a readable memory region of at least nbyte bytes; since the parameter is not const, callers should not assume the buffer remains unmodified by this function (conservative assumption due to unknowns).
nbyte may be zero; behavior should be consistent with underlying OS write semantics (unknown specifics).
The current file offset is advanced by the number of bytes written (inferred from typical write semantics).
Error reporting conventions (e.g., negative return, errno) are not specified; callers must handle unknown conventions.

functions.name: seek_file
functions.signature: int64_t seek_file(file_t fd, int64_t offset, int whence);
functions.description: Changes the file offset for fd according to offset and whence, returning the resulting file position. Cross-platform wrapper similar to lseek/lseek64. whence is expected to accept SEEK_SET, SEEK_CUR, or SEEK_END semantics; exact accepted values are not documented here.
requirements: fd must be a valid, open file handle.
whence must be a valid seek origin as supported by the implementation (typically SEEK_SET, SEEK_CUR, SEEK_END).
offset may be negative when used with SEEK_CUR or SEEK_END; the resulting position must remain valid for the underlying file (general constraint; exact bounds not specified).
On success, the return value is the new absolute file offset; on failure, a negative value or sentinel may be returned (exact error conventions unspecified).

functions.name: fstat_file
functions.description: Retrieves metadata for an open file handle fd and stores it into fs. file_stat_t contains file_size, mtime, ctime, atime (all uint64_t), and mode (uint32_t). Cross-platform wrapper around fstat/GetFileInformationByHandle. Return value semantics are not documented here.
requirements: fd must be a valid, open file handle.
fs must be a non-null pointer to a writeable file_stat_t structure.
Timestamps are returned as uint64_t; the epoch and units (e.g., seconds vs. nanoseconds) are not specified.
Return/error codes are not specified; callers must handle unknown conventions.

functions.name: stat_file
functions.description: Retrieves metadata for the file at path and stores it into fs without requiring the file to be open. Cross-platform wrapper around stat/GetFileAttributesEx or similar. file_stat_t fields are as defined in the header. Return value semantics are not documented here.
requirements: path must be a non-null, null-terminated string referring to an accessible filesystem object.
fs must be a non-null pointer to a writeable file_stat_t structure.
Timestamps units/epoch and mode value semantics are not specified.
Return/error codes are not specified; callers must handle unknown conventions.

functions.name: _memset
functions.description: Sets a memory region starting at m to a fixed value for n bytes. Because no value parameter is provided, this function is presumed to zero-fill the memory (memset with value 0). Exact behavior is inferred; documentation is not provided in the header.
requirements: m must be a non-null pointer to a writable memory region of at least n bytes.
n may be zero; the function will then perform no writes.
The fill value is presumed to be zero due to the signature lacking a value parameter; callers should verify this assumption against the implementation if available.

functions.name: _memcpy
functions.description: Copies n bytes from src to dst. This is a wrapper around memory copy functionality resembling memcpy, but with non-const parameters and a void return. Behavior on overlapping regions is unspecified; typical memcpy behavior treats overlap as undefined. Exact behavior is inferred from the name and signature; documentation is not provided in the header.
requirements: dst must be a non-null pointer to a writable memory region of at least n bytes.
src must be a non-null pointer to a readable memory region of at least n bytes.
Behavior for overlapping regions is unspecified; callers should avoid overlap to be safe.
n may be zero; the function will then perform no writes.

functions.name: BE16
functions.description: Converts a 16-bit unsigned integer between host byte order and big-endian representation. On big-endian hosts it returns x unchanged; on little-endian hosts it swaps the byte order. Use when serializing to or deserializing from big-endian (network-order) data to ensure consistent behavior across architectures.
requirements: x is a 16-bit unsigned integer value in host byte order.
No side effects or error reporting; the return value is the converted result.
Can be called for any 16-bit value within [0, 65535].
Header must be included so the static inline definition is visible to the caller.

requirements: x is a 32-bit unsigned integer value in host byte order.
No side effects or error reporting; the return value is the converted result.

functions.name: get_normal_color
functions.description: Captures the current console text attributes on Windows so they can be restored later with set_normal_color. On non-Windows platforms it is a no-op. Note: if NO_COLOR is defined at compile time, get_normal_color is a macro that takes one dummy argument and does nothing.
requirements: Windows: Requires a valid console STD_OUTPUT_HANDLE; behavior is meaningful only when a console is attached.
Call this before the first call to set_normal_color on Windows to ensure attributes are saved for restoration.
Not thread-safe: uses a shared static CONSOLE_SCREEN_BUFFER_INFO; concurrent calls may race.

Build-time variability: If NO_COLOR is defined, this symbol is a macro of the form get_normal_color(x) that does nothing; callers must either provide a dummy argument in that build or avoid defining NO_COLOR when using the function form.

functions.name: set_normal_color
functions.description: Restores the previously saved console text attributes on Windows (as captured by get_normal_color). On non-Windows platforms, emits the ANSI escape sequence "\033[0;37m" to reset to a normal/white-like text color. Note: if NO_COLOR is defined at compile time, set_normal_color is a macro that takes one dummy argument and does nothing.
requirements: Windows: Must call get_normal_color() earlier in the process to have valid attributes to restore; otherwise the restored attributes are unspecified.
Windows: Requires a valid console STD_OUTPUT_HANDLE; effective only when a console is attached.
Non-Windows: The output stream must accept ANSI escape sequences for the color change to take effect (typically an ANSI-capable terminal).
Not thread-safe: relies on shared static state captured by get_normal_color.

Build-time variability: If NO_COLOR is defined, this symbol is a macro of the form set_normal_color(x) that does nothing; callers must either provide a dummy argument in that build or avoid defining NO_COLOR when using the function form.

functions.name: set_white_text

On non-Windows platforms, emits the ANSI escape sequence "\033[1;37m". Note: if NO_COLOR is defined at compile time, set_white_text is a macro that takes one dummy argument and does nothing.
requirements: Windows: Effective only when a console is attached; uses STD_OUTPUT_HANDLE.
Non-Windows: The output stream should be an ANSI-capable terminal to display the color change.

Build-time variability: If NO_COLOR is defined, this symbol is a macro of the form set_white_text(x) that does nothing; callers must either provide a dummy argument in that build or avoid defining NO_COLOR when using the function form.

Note: if NO_COLOR is defined at compile time, set_red_text is a macro that takes one dummy argument and does nothing.
requirements: Windows: Effective only when a console is attached; uses STD_OUTPUT_HANDLE.
Non-Windows: The output stream should be an ANSI-capable terminal to display the color change.

Build-time variability: If NO_COLOR is defined, this symbol is a macro of the form set_red_text(x) that does nothing; callers must either provide a dummy argument in that build or avoid defining NO_COLOR when using the function form.

Note: if NO_COLOR is defined at compile time, set_gray_text is a macro that takes one dummy argument and does nothing.
requirements: Windows: Effective only when a console is attached; uses STD_OUTPUT_HANDLE.

functions.name: _memset
functions.description: Zero-fill helper that writes n bytes to the memory region starting at m. Because there is no value parameter (unlike standard memset), the function most likely clears the buffer to 0. Use to initialize or clear a block of memory of length n bytes. Return type is void; no error reporting is provided.
requirements: m must point to a writable memory region of at least n bytes.
n specifies the number of bytes to write; it must not exceed the allocated size of the region pointed to by m.
The exact value written is not documented; based on the missing value parameter, it is presumed to write zeros to all n bytes (unknown if any other pattern is used).
Behavior when m is NULL (e.g., if n == 0) is not documented; callers should pass a valid non-NULL pointer.
Thread-safety and reentrancy characteristics are not documented; avoid concurrent writes to the same region.

functions.name: _memcpy
functions.description: Copies n bytes of data from src to dst. Unlike standard memcpy, src is not const, but the intent is consistent with a raw byte-wise copy. Use to transfer a fixed number of bytes between memory regions. Return type is void; no error reporting is provided.
requirements: dst must point to a writable memory region of at least n bytes.
src must point to a readable memory region of at least n bytes.
dst and src should not be the same pointer unless n is 0; overlapping region behavior is not documented and should be assumed unsafe (use only non-overlapping regions).
n specifies the number of bytes to copy; it must not exceed the allocated sizes of the respective regions.
Passing NULL for dst or src is not documented, even when n == 0; callers should pass valid non-NULL pointers.
The function does not indicate errors; callers must ensure preconditions to avoid undefined behavior.
Thread-safety is not documented; avoid concurrent modification of src or dst during the call.

functions.name: padlock_supports
functions.description: Detects whether the current CPU supports a given VIA PadLock feature (e.g., AES engine, RNG). Returns 1 if the feature is supported, 0 otherwise. Typical usage: call before using PadLock-accelerated routines to gate hardware usage.
requirements: feature should be one of the PADLOCK_* feature masks (e.g., PADLOCK_RNG, PADLOCK_ACE, PADLOCK_PHE, PADLOCK_PMM) or a valid combination thereof
Function availability depends on being built for x86 with GNU C and assembler support as guarded by the header’s build macros; otherwise this API may be unavailable at compile time

functions.name: padlock_xcryptecb
functions.signature: int padlock_xcryptecb( aes_context *ctx, int mode, const unsigned char input[16], unsigned char output[16] );
functions.description: Performs a single-block AES ECB encrypt/decrypt using the VIA PadLock hardware engine. Returns 0 on success, 1 on failure. Use after setting up an AES key in ctx. ECB processes exactly one 16-byte block per call.
requirements: ctx must be a valid, initialized AES context with an AES key already set

import os
import random
import string
from typing import List

# Generator for valid filesystem paths to be consumed by FUZZ_PARAM_FILENAME.
# The fuzzer runtime will create a file at the provided path and fill it with
# arbitrary data. Our job is to supply a path string buffer that is syntactically
# valid and likely to exercise different code paths via flags and file name shapes.

SAFE_CHARS = string.ascii_letters + string.digits
EXTRA_CHARS = "-_.+ ,()[]{}!@#%&=^$"  # Common but safe-ish extras for filenames

def _rand_name(rng: random.Random, min_len: int, max_len: int) -> str:
    n = rng.randint(min_len, max_len)
    # Mix safe chars with extras to cover more path parsing cases
    alphabet = SAFE_CHARS + EXTRA_CHARS
    return "".join(rng.choice(alphabet) for _ in range(n)).strip()

def _rand_ext(rng: random.Random) -> str:
    # ISO/PS3-related and generic extensions to steer implementations that branch by ext
    exts = [
        "iso", "bin", "img", "ird", "zip", "gz", "txt", "dat",
        "ISO", "Iso",  # case-variance
    ]
    return rng.choice(exts)

def _rand_components(rng: random.Random) -> List[str]:
    # Build 1-4 path components to exercise directory traversal without using ..
    count = rng.randint(1, 4)
    comps = []
    for i in range(count):
        base = _rand_name(rng, 3, 12)
        # Occasionally insert spaces or leading/trailing dots to test handling
        if rng.random() < 0.2:
            base = (" " if rng.random() < 0.5 else "") + base
        if rng.random() < 0.2:
            base = base + ("." if rng.random() < 0.5 else " ")
        # Avoid empty components
        base = base.replace(os.sep, "-")
        comps.append(base)
    return comps

def _compose_path(rng: random.Random) -> str:
    # Construct a syntactically valid path for both POSIX and Windows. The fuzzer
    # runtime will interpret it on the host OS, so we try to keep it portable.

    # Pick a root style: relative subdir inside fuzzer workspace
    # We prefix with "fuzz/" style directory to hint the runtime to place the file there.
    root_choices = ["fuzz", "tmp", "work", "data", "iso"]
    root = rng.choice(root_choices)

    comps = [root] + _rand_components(rng)

    filename_core = _rand_name(rng, 4, 16)
    # Occasionally form names that resemble PS3 ISO or game codes
    if rng.random() < 0.35:
        # e.g., BLUS12345-My Game
        prefix = rng.choice(["BLUS", "BCUS", "BLES", "BCES", "NPUB", "NPEB"]) + str(rng.randint(10000, 99999))
        filename_core = prefix + ("-" if rng.random() < 0.7 else "_") + filename_core

    # Optional extension
    if rng.random() < 0.9:
        filename = f"{filename_core}.{_rand_ext(rng)}"
    else:
        filename = filename_core

    comps.append(filename)

    path = os.sep.join(comps)

    # Ensure final path is not excessively long and contains no forbidden characters
    # Replace any accidental separators from EXTRA_CHARS if present (defensive)
    path = path.replace("\\", os.sep).replace("/", os.sep)
    # Collapse duplicate separators
    while os.sep*2 in path:
        path = path.replace(os.sep*2, os.sep)

    # Bound length to something reasonable to avoid OS path limits in some environments
    if len(path) > 300:
        path = path[:300]
    # Ensure it ends with a filename-like component
    if path.endswith(os.sep):
        path = path[:-1]

    return path

def _encode_c_string(s: str) -> bytes:
    # Encode as UTF-8 and add trailing NUL to mimic C-string expectations
    return s.encode('utf-8', errors='ignore') + b"\x00"

def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)

    # We only need to supply a valid filesystem path for FUZZ_PARAM_FILENAME().
    # The fuzzer stubs also call FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int) for flags, which the
    # framework supplies separately; our buffer should therefore concentrate on
    # a single path blob. Some frameworks will reuse the provided buffer for
    # multiple FUZZ_PARAM_* pulls; to make that robust, we can pack multiple
    # NUL-terminated candidate paths back-to-back so the harness can choose the
    # first, and later pulls still see valid strings if it advances internally.

    num_candidates = rng.randint(1, 4)
    paths = []
    for _ in range(num_candidates):
        p = _compose_path(rng)
        paths.append(_encode_c_string(p))

    blob = b"".join(paths)

    # Guarantee size constraint
    if len(blob) > 4096:
        blob = blob[:4095] + b"\x00"

    # Ensure there is at least one NUL terminator
    if not blob or blob[-1] != 0:
        blob += b"\x00"

    return blob

import os
import random
import struct
from typing import List

# This generator produces an opaque binary blob intended to be used as the data buffer
# for write operations in the provided fuzzing stubs. It focuses on generating
# interesting, valid byte patterns and lengths aligned with the stubs' bounds
# (0..2048 for AbstractFile::write, up to 2048 for File::write, up to 1024 for VIsoFile::write).
# The output is a bytes object with size chosen from a curated set to exercise
# different behaviors: zeros, printable text, high-entropy data, repeating patterns,
# edge lengths, power-of-two sizes, and alignment-straddling sizes.

_MAX_TOTAL = 4096  # global hard cap per instructions

def _biased_lengths(rng: random.Random) -> List[int]:
    # Include edge and typical sizes for the three stubs: 0..2048 and 0..1024
    corpus = set()
    # General edges
    edges = [0, 1, 15, 16, 17, 31, 32, 63, 64, 127, 128, 255, 256, 511, 512, 767, 768, 1023, 1024, 1536, 1792, 2047, 2048]
    corpus.update(edges)
    # Powers of two up to 2048
    for p in [2, 4, 8, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048]:
        corpus.add(p)
        if p > 1:
            corpus.add(p - 1)
            corpus.add(p + 1 if p + 1 <= 2048 else 2048)
    # Some random sizes within limits
    for _ in range(10):
        corpus.add(rng.randint(0, 2048))
    # Keep within bounds and sorted
    sizes = sorted(x for x in corpus if 0 <= x <= 2048)
    # Randomly select one, but weight toward interesting edges by sampling from the list directly
    # We’ll return a small list of candidate lengths to combine with multiple patterns below
    rng.shuffle(sizes)
    return sizes[:rng.randint(5, 12)]

def _pattern_zero(n: int) -> bytes:
    return b"\x00" * n

def _pattern_ones(n: int) -> bytes:
    return b"\xFF" * n

def _pattern_increment(n: int, start: int = 0) -> bytes:
    return bytes((start + i) & 0xFF for i in range(n))

def _pattern_repeat(seq: bytes, n: int) -> bytes:
    if not seq:
        return b"\x00" * n
    return (seq * (n // len(seq) + 1))[:n]

def _pattern_ascii(n: int, rng: random.Random) -> bytes:
    # Mix of printable ASCII and newlines/tabs
    alphabet = (list(range(0x20, 0x7E)) + [0x09, 0x0A, 0x0D])
    return bytes(rng.choice(alphabet) for _ in range(n))

def _pattern_utf8_text(n: int, rng: random.Random) -> bytes:
    # Compose plausible UTF-8 chunks then trim/pad
    words = [
        "Lorem", "ipsum", "dolor", "sit", "amet", "PS3", "ISO", "Joliet", "AES",
        "padding", "sector", "block", "file", "write", "test", "data"
    ]
    s = []
    while sum(len(x) for x in s) < n:
        w = rng.choice(words)
        s.append(w)
        if rng.random() < 0.4:
            s.append(" ")
        if rng.random() < 0.2:
            s.append("\n")
    b = ("".join(s)).encode("utf-8")
    if len(b) >= n:
        return b[:n]
    return b + b"\x00" * (n - len(b))

def _pattern_high_entropy(n: int, rng: random.Random) -> bytes:
    return bytes(rng.getrandbits(8) for _ in range(n))

def _pattern_structured(n: int, rng: random.Random) -> bytes:
    # Build a header-like region then fill remainder with patterned data
    # Header: magic + length + checksum placeholder
    magic = b"BUF0"
    length = struct.pack("<I", n)
    header = magic + length
    remain = max(0, n - len(header))
    body = _pattern_repeat(b"\xAA\x55\xAA\x55", remain // 2) + _pattern_increment(remain - (remain // 2), start=rng.randrange(256))
    out = (header + body)[:n]
    return out

def _build_variants(n: int, rng: random.Random) -> List[bytes]:
    patterns = []
    patterns.append(_pattern_zero(n))
    if n > 0:
        patterns.append(_pattern_ones(n))
        patterns.append(_pattern_increment(n, start=rng.randrange(256)))
        patterns.append(_pattern_repeat(b"ABCD", n))
        patterns.append(_pattern_ascii(n, rng))
        patterns.append(_pattern_utf8_text(n, rng))
        patterns.append(_pattern_high_entropy(n, rng))
        patterns.append(_pattern_structured(n, rng))
        # Sector-aligned pattern (2048) repeated/truncated
        patterns.append(_pattern_repeat(bytes([i & 0xFF for i in range(256)]), n))
    return patterns

def _choose_and_mix(patterns: List[bytes], rng: random.Random) -> bytes:
    if not patterns:
        return b""
    # Choose one pattern or concatenate a couple small ones, keeping total <= 2048 and <= _MAX_TOTAL
    choice = rng.random()
    if choice < 0.6:
        return rng.choice(patterns)
    else:
        out = bytearray()
        rng.shuffle(patterns)
        for p in patterns:
            if len(out) + len(p) > 2048:
                break
            out.extend(p)
            if rng.random() < 0.4:
                break
        return bytes(out[:2048])

def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    lengths = _biased_lengths(rng)
    n = rng.choice(lengths) if lengths else rng.randint(0, 2048)
    # Build variants and pick/mix
    variants = _build_variants(n, rng)
    data = _choose_and_mix(variants, rng)
    # Ensure final size within the allowed caps; empty is fine for zero-length writes
    if len(data) > _MAX_TOTAL:
        data = data[:_MAX_TOTAL]
    return data
